sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: A Carotid Cavernous Fistula (CCF) is an acquired or congenital communication between the carotid artery (or its dural branches) and the cavernous sinus. This creates a high-pressure arterial flow into a low-pressure venous system, leading to venous congestion, ocular hypertension, and potential vision loss.

rows: Meningeal branches of the External Carotid (ECA)
Meningeal branches of BOTH ICA and ECA

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Hemodynamics
content: 1. Arterial-Venous Communication: High-pressure blood bypasses capillary bed.
2. Venous Arterialization: Episcleral and orbital veins become engorged and tortuous.
3. Reduced Outflow: Elevated episcleral venous pressure (EVP) impairs aqueous humor drainage.
4. Orbital Congestion: Leads to proptosis, chemosis, and extraocular muscle edema.
5. Ischemic Cascade: Decreased ocular perfusion pressure (OPP) leads to retinal and optic nerve ischemia.

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Classic Triad
content: Pulsatile Proptosis: Often associated with a palpable thrill.
Conjunctival Chemosis: Significant 'corkscrew' epibulbar vessel arterialization.
Orbital Bruit: Subjective (whooshing heard by patient) or objective (audible via stethoscope over the temple).

branches: Anterior: Arterialized 'corkscrew' vessels, Chemosis, Raised IOP (EVP > 10mmHg)
Extraocular: CN III, IV, VI palsies (VI most common due to position in CS)
Fundus: Venous tortuosity, Retinal hemorrhages, Disc edema, Choroidal effusions
Vision: Decreased VA due to Glaucoma, Exposure Keratopathy, or ON Ischemia

rows: Lid retraction, no bruit, no corkscrew vessels
Fever, elevated WBC, pain on movement
Sinusitis on CT; orbital fat stranding
Involvement of EOM tendons and fat

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Non-Invasive Screening: B-Scan USG (demonstrates dilated Superior Ophthalmic Vein [SOV]).
2. CT/MRI: Shows enlarged EOMs, dilated SOV, and bowing of the cavernous sinus wall.
3. MRA/CTA: Useful for visualizing the shunt, but may miss low-flow indirect CCFs.
4. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): THE GOLD STANDARD. Required for definitive diagnosis and planning treatment.
5. Tonometry: Tonopen/Goldmann to assess EVP-related ocular hypertension.

sections.title: Medical & Conservative Management
content: Observation: Appropriate for low-flow (Type B-D) shunts as up to 70% may spontaneously close.
IOP Control: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, or CAIs (Avoid Miotics).
Lubrication: Intensive artificial tears/ointments for exposure keratopathy.
Carotid Massage: Intermittent compression of the carotid artery to induce thrombosis (Use with caution!).

branches: Transvenous Embolization: Preferred for Indirect shunts (via Inferior Petrosal Sinus)
Transarterial Embolization: Usually for Direct Type A (Detachable coils/Onyx)
Direct SOV Access: Surgical cut-down to SOV when venous routes are occluded
Stereotactic Radiosurgery: Reserved for refractory low-flow dural shunts

sections.title: RED FLAGS: Neurosurgical Emergencies
content: Rapidly progressive vision loss (Ischemic Optic Neuropathy or Glaucoma)
Intractable retro-orbital pain
Evidence of cortical venous reflux on angiography (High risk of Intracranial Hemorrhage)
Rapidly expanding proptosis with exposure-related corneal melt

content.explanation: P: Pulsatile proptosis; U: Unilateral (usually); L: Loud bruit; S: Shunt (A-V); E: Elevated IOP/Episcleral venous pressure.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
content: Secondary Glaucoma: Most common cause of permanent vision loss.
Venous Stasis Retinopathy: Mimics CRVO but with high EVP.
Intracranial Hemorrhage: Risk associated with dural shunts and cortical venous drainage.
Prognosis: Excellent if treated timely; Indirect shunts often resolve with minimal intervention.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: The 6th Nerve (Abducens) is the most commonly affected CN because it lies centrally within the cavernous sinus.
Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome Type IV (Vascular type) is a major risk factor for spontaneous direct CCF.
Gold Standard for diagnosis is always Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA).
Post-traumatic CCF (Type A) is usually high-flow and requires urgent endovascular intervention.
Indirect shunts in post-menopausal women are often mistaken for chronic conjunctivitis or thyroid eye disease.

sections.title: Recent Advances
sections.content: The shift from surgical ligation to endovascular techniques has revolutionized CCF management. The use of liquid embolic agents like Onyx and sophisticated microcatheters has increased the success rate of transvenous approaches to >90% for complex dural shunts. Recent studies emphasize the importance of identifying 'cortical venous reflux' as a primary indicator for aggressive treatment to prevent stroke.
